questions.question: What must be checked to show that a subspace U is invariant under a linear operator A?
options: Every vector in V is sent into U by A.
Every vector in U is fixed pointwise by A.
Every vector u in U is sent back into U by A.
Every vector outside U is sent to zero.

questions.question: Does an invariant subspace have to consist only of eigenvectors?
options: No. It only has to be closed under the action of A.
Yes, but only for diagonal matrices.
No. It does not even need to be a subspace.
Yes. Every nonzero vector in it must be an eigenvector.

questions.question: Why is the span of an eigenvector p invariant under A?
options: Because $Ap=λp$ remains in the same one-dimensional span.
Because $Ap=0$ for every eigenvector.
Because eigenvectors are never scaled by A.
Because every vector in V lies in span(p).

questions.question: Which subspaces are always listed as basic invariant subspaces for a linear operator A?
options: Only eigenspaces with positive eigenvalues.
${0}$, V, $ker A$, and $range A$.
Only ${0}$ and no other subspace.
All subsets of V, whether or not they are subspaces.

questions.question: What is the geometric idea behind an invariant subspace?
options: The operator sends every vector to a perpendicular vector.
The subspace contains no nonzero vector.
The subspace changes dimension after applying A.
The operator never sends that part of the space outside itself.

questions.question: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$, is the x-axis invariant?
options: No, A sends $(x,0)$ to $(0,3x)$.
No, diagonal matrices have no invariant axes.
Only if x is positive.
Yes, A sends $(x,0)$ to $(2x,0)$.

questions.question: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, is the line $span((1,1)^T)$ invariant?
options: No, A sends it to $(1,-1)^T$.
Yes, A sends $(1,1)^T$ to itself.
No, a line is invariant only for diagonal matrices.
Only if the scalar multiplying $(1,1)^T$ is zero.

questions.question: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, is the x-axis invariant?
options: No, A sends $(1,0)^T$ to $(0,1)^T$.
Yes, because A is square.
Only if the field is complex.
Yes, because every line through the origin is invariant.

questions.question: Let A be any linear operator. Why is $ker A$ invariant under A?
options: If $u∈ker A$, then $Au=0$, and $0∈ker A$.
If $u∈ker A$, then $Au=u$, so $u∈ker A$.
The kernel is invariant because it equals V for every A.
The kernel is invariant only when A is invertible.

questions.question: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, is $span((1,0)^T)$ invariant?
options: No, A sends it to $(1,1)^T$.
Only if the scalar is 1.
Yes, A sends $(1,0)^T$ to $(1,0)^T$.
No, only eigenspaces of diagonal matrices are invariant.

questions.question: If U is invariant under A, what does the restriction of A to U mean?
options: A maps U onto the whole space V.
A must vanish on U.
A stops being linear on U.
A can be viewed as an operator from U to U.

questions.question: Why is range A invariant under A for a linear operator A on V?
options: If y=Ax, then Ay must be zero.
Range A is invariant because every vector is in the kernel.
If y=Ax, then Ay=A(Ax), which is again an output of A.
Range A is invariant only when A is diagonalizable.

questions.question: Can a subspace U be invariant even if A is not the identity on U?
options: Yes. A may move vectors inside U without fixing them.
No. Invariant means fixed pointwise.
No. Invariant means A sends U to zero.
Yes, but only when U is not a subspace, under all circumstances whatsoever.

questions.question: Let A be rotation by 90 degrees in $R^2$. Is the x-axis invariant?
options: No, the x-axis is sent to the y-axis.
Yes, because rotations preserve lengths.
Yes, because the x-axis is a subspace.
Only if the vector has length 1.

questions.question: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, what is $range A$?
Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ and $U=span((1,1)^T)$. Is U invariant?
options: Only if 2 and 3 are both nonzero.
Yes, because every one-dimensional subspace is invariant.
Yes, because A is diagonal.
No, because $A(1,1)^T=(2,3)^T$ is not a multiple of $(1,1)^T$.

questions.question: For a one-dimensional subspace $span(p)$ with $p≠0$, what does invariance under A amount to?
options: P is orthogonal to $Ap$.
P is an eigenvector of A.
P lies in $ker A$ only.
P has norm 1.

questions.question: Why is $\ker A$ invariant under a linear operator $A$?
options: If $u\in\ker A$, then $Au=0$, and $0\in\ker A$
Every $u\in\ker A$ satisfies $Au=u$
$\ker A$ always equals $\operatorname{range}A$
$A$ must be invertible whenever its kernel is invariant

questions.question: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, is $span((0,1)^T)$ invariant?
options: No, because $A(0,1)^T=(1,1)^T$ is not in $span((0,1)^T)$.
Only if the scalar multiplying $(0,1)^T$ is zero.
Yes, because every coordinate axis is invariant for upper triangular matrices.
Yes, because the matrix has eigenvalue 1.

questions.question: Let U be the plane $z=0$ in $R^3$ and $A(x,y,z)=(x+y,y,2z)$. Is U invariant?
options: Yes, if z=0 then the third coordinate of A(x,y,z) is also 0.
Only for vectors with x=y.
No, because A is not the identity on U.
No, because the first coordinate changes, for every possible choice of input.
